title: async/await patterns
summary: Sequential versus parallel awaits, Promise.all, allSettled, race and any, the async forEach trap, bounded concurrency, retries with backoff and cancellation with AbortController.
lesson:
## Sequential versus parallel

```js
// sequential: ~200 ms (each await waits for the previous one)
const user = await getUser(id);
const prefs = await getPrefs(id);

// parallel: ~100 ms (both start before either is awaited)
const [user, prefs] = await Promise.all([getUser(id), getPrefs(id)]);
```

Await in sequence only when a call needs the previous result. Independent calls should start together.

A case: a dashboard that awaits five independent 80 ms calls one after another takes 400 ms; started together it takes about 80 ms, the time of the slowest call. The calls must be started before the first `await`: `const p = getUser(id)` starts the work, and `await p` only waits for it.

## The four combinators

- `Promise.all(ps)`: fulfils with an array of values in INPUT order; rejects as soon as ANY rejects (fail-fast; the other operations keep running, their results are ignored).
- `Promise.allSettled(ps)`: always fulfils, with `{ status: 'fulfilled', value }` / `{ status: 'rejected', reason }` per input. Use it for "send all notifications, report which failed".
- `Promise.race(ps)`: settles like the FIRST promise to settle, fulfilled or rejected (timeouts, topic 12).
- `Promise.any(ps)`: fulfils with the first FULFILMENT; rejects with an `AggregateError` (with `.errors`) only if all reject. Use it for "try three mirrors, take the first that works".

## The async forEach trap

```js
items.forEach(async (item) => { await save(item); });
console.log('done');   // runs BEFORE any save finished; errors become unhandled rejections
```

`forEach` ignores the promises its callback returns. Use `for (const item of items) await save(item)` for sequential work, or `await Promise.all(items.map(save))` for parallel.

`map` has the same shape but at least returns the promises, which is why wrapping it in `Promise.all` works. A rejection inside a forEach callback has nobody awaiting it, so it surfaces as an unhandled rejection, and since Node 15 that ends the process with exit code 1.

## Bounded concurrency

`Promise.all(ids.map(fetch))` over 10,000 ids starts 10,000 requests at once and gets you rate-limited. Limit how many run at a time: keep N "workers" that each pull the next item until the list is empty. Libraries like p-limit do this; it is a common interview exercise.

## Retries with backoff

Retry only **transient** failures (timeouts, 503, connection resets), never validation errors. Wait longer each time (exponential backoff: 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms), add random **jitter** so clients do not retry in lockstep, and cap the number of attempts. Retried writes must be **idempotent** (an idempotency key on POST /payments).

## Cancellation with AbortController

```js
const ac = new AbortController();
const res = await fetch(url, { signal: ac.signal });   // ac.abort() rejects with an AbortError
await fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2000) }); // built-in timeout signal
```

Pass a signal down through your own async functions and check `signal.aborted` (or listen for `'abort'`) so work stops when a client disconnects or a user navigates away.

An aborted `fetch` rejects with a `DOMException` named `AbortError`, and one cancelled by `AbortSignal.timeout` rejects with one named `TimeoutError`, so a `catch` can tell "the user gave up" from "the call was too slow". A signal fires only once: create a new controller for each new request.

## Error handling

`try/catch` around `await` catches rejections. With `Promise.all`, one try/catch catches the first failure; use `allSettled` when you need every outcome. Never leave a promise un-awaited unless you attach a `.catch`.

A trap: `try { return save(x); } catch { ... }` inside an async function catches nothing, because the promise is returned before it rejects and the rejection reaches the caller. Write `return await save(x)` when the catch block should handle it.

quiz.prompt: Two independent 100 ms calls: `const a = await f(); const b = await g();` takes about how long?
choices: 100 ms
200 ms
50 ms
150 ms
quiz.explanation: Each `await` suspends the function until that promise settles, and `g()` is not even called until the line before it has finished. The two 100 ms waits therefore add up instead of overlapping. Starting both first, `const pa = f(), pb = g();`, and then awaiting `Promise.all([pa, pb])` lets the waits overlap and takes about 100 ms. Nothing here makes either call faster, so 50 ms is not possible.

choices: Rejects with "boom" as soon as it rejects
Waits for all three, then rejects with "boom"
Fulfils with [1, undefined, 3] once all settle
Fulfils with [1, 3], skipping the failure
quiz.explanation: `Promise.all` settles its own promise from the first rejection it sees and does not wait for the slower inputs, so it never waits for all three. The other operations are not cancelled: slowOk(3) keeps running and its value is dropped. It also never fulfils with a hole like `undefined` or silently skips a failure. When every outcome matters, use the combinator that reports each one.

quiz.prompt: Which combinator ALWAYS fulfils and reports each outcome?
choices: `Promise.all`
`Promise.race`
`Promise.allSettled`
`Promise.any`
quiz.explanation: It waits until every input has settled and fulfils with one record per input, in input order: `{ status: 'fulfilled', value }` or `{ status: 'rejected', reason }`. A rejection never escapes it, so there is nothing to catch. `Promise.race` copies whichever input settles first, a rejection included, and `Promise.all` rejects on the first failure, so neither is guaranteed to fulfil.

quiz.prompt: What does `Promise.any` reject with when every input rejects?
choices: The first error, as soon as it arrives
The last error, after every input settles
A TypeError saying no promise fulfilled
An AggregateError holding all the errors
quiz.explanation: `Promise.any` treats a rejection as "try the next one", so no single failure settles it. Only when the last input has rejected does it give up, and because no one reason explains the failure, it rejects with a single object whose `.errors` array lists every reason in input order, with the message "All promises were rejected". It is neither the first nor the last error alone, and no TypeError is involved.

quiz.prompt: `items.forEach(async (i) => { await save(i); }); console.log("done");` When does "done" print?
choices: After every save has finished
Before the saves finish
When the forEach promise resolves
After the first save
quiz.explanation: `forEach` calls the callback for each item and discards its return value. An async callback returns a pending promise at its first `await`, so forEach starts every save and returns `undefined` straight away; there is no forEach promise to wait on. The `console.log` then runs while the saves are still pending. Use `for...of` with `await`, or `await Promise.all(items.map(save))`.

quiz.prompt: Which failures should an automatic retry handle?
choices: Transient ones: timeouts, 503s, connection resets
Validation failures like 400s and 422s from the API
Authorization failures like 401s and 403s
Business-rule rejections like insufficient funds
quiz.explanation: A retry only helps when the same request can succeed on the next attempt. A timeout, a 503 or a reset connection describes the network or the server at that moment, which may change a second later. A 400 or 422 validation error, a 401 or 403, or an insufficient-funds rejection describes the request itself, so sending it again returns the same answer and only adds load.

quiz.prompt: Why add random jitter to retry delays?
choices: To keep the overall retry time under the timeout
Because HTTP requires clients to randomise retry delays
So clients that failed together do not retry in lockstep
To hide retries from the server's rate limiter
quiz.explanation: Clients that hit the same outage compute the same backoff schedule, so without jitter they all come back at 100, 200 and 400 ms at the same instant. Those synchronised bursts are a thundering herd that knocks the recovering service down again. Random jitter spreads the attempts out. HTTP does not require it, and it does nothing to hide retries from a rate limiter; it only smooths the load.

quiz.prompt: What makes a retried POST /payments safe?
choices: A longer client timeout, so the first attempt completes
A unique request id generated afresh on every retry
An idempotency key the server deduplicates on
Limiting the client to at most two retries per request
quiz.explanation: A lost response leaves the client unsure whether the charge happened, so it must be able to resend safely. The client generates one key per payment and sends that same key on every retry; the server stores the outcome under the key and returns it again instead of charging twice. A fresh request id per retry defeats this, since every attempt looks new, and a longer timeout or a retry cap only makes duplicates rarer.

quiz.prompt: Which API cancels an in-flight fetch?
choices: clearTimeout on the timer id that fetch returns
An AbortController signal, then controller.abort()
Promise.race against a promise that rejects on timeout
Deleting the promise variable so it is collected
quiz.explanation: A promise has no cancel method, so the operation itself has to accept a cancellation channel. `fetch` takes a `signal` option and listens to it; aborting stops the request and rejects the fetch with a DOMException named `AbortError`. Racing against a timeout only stops you waiting while the request keeps running, fetch returns no timer id to clear, and deleting the variable does not close the socket.

quiz.prompt: Fetching 10,000 URLs with `Promise.all(urls.map(fetch))` is risky because...
choices: Promise.all rejects arrays with more than 2^16 entries
Promise.all returns results in completion order, not input order
fetch runs the requests one at a time, so the batch is slow
Every request starts at once and floods sockets and rate limits
quiz.explanation: `urls.map(fetch)` calls fetch 10,000 times in one synchronous loop, so all of them are in flight before the first response arrives. `Promise.all` accepts far more than 2^16 entries and keeps results in input order; the problem is the load, not the combinator. Bound it with a pool of N workers that each take the next URL when they finish, which keeps throughput high without tripping the server's limits.

flashcards.front: When should awaits run in sequence?
flashcards.back: Only when a call needs the previous call's result. Independent work should start together and be awaited with Promise.all.
all fails fast on the first rejection and gives values in input order; allSettled waits for everything and reports every fulfilment and rejection.
race settles like whichever input settles first, even a rejection; any waits for the first fulfilment and only fails if all fail.

flashcards.front: Why is an async callback in forEach a bug?
flashcards.back: forEach discards the returned promises, so nothing waits for them and their errors go unhandled.
Start a fixed number of workers; each repeatedly takes the next unprocessed item until none remain, writing results back by index.

flashcards.front: The ingredients of a good retry policy
flashcards.back: Retry only transient failures, wait exponentially longer with jitter, cap the attempts, and make the operation idempotent.

flashcards.front: How do you cancel async work in JavaScript?
flashcards.back: Pass an AbortSignal down the call chain; abort() rejects signal-aware APIs like fetch, and your code checks signal.aborted.
A signal that aborts itself after the given milliseconds, a one-line timeout for fetch and other signal-aware APIs.

drills.title: mapLimit: async map with bounded concurrency
drills.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "We resize 5,000 images with an external API that allows 4 concurrent requests. Write the helper."

**Why it matters.** `Promise.all(items.map(fn))` starts everything at once. A small pool of workers that pull the next item when they finish keeps exactly N calls in flight and still returns results in input order.

**Your task.** Export `mapLimit(items, limit, fn)`. It returns a promise of an array where element i is the result of `await fn(items[i], i)`, and:
- at most `limit` calls of `fn` are in flight at any moment
- results are in INPUT order, whatever order the calls finish in
- if any call rejects, the returned promise rejects with that reason (calls already started may finish, but no NEW call starts after the failure)
- an empty `items` array resolves to `[]`

`limit` is a whole number of 1 or more.

**Worked example.** With items `[30, 10, 20]` (each `fn` waits that many ms and returns it) and limit 2, the result is `[30, 10, 20]`, and never more than 2 calls overlap.

tests.name: results keep input order
never more than limit calls in flight
fn receives the item and its index
tests.code: assert.deepEqual(await mod.mapLimit(['a', 'b'], 1, async (s, i) => s + i), ['a0', 'b1']);

tests.name: a failure rejects and starts no new calls
an empty list resolves to [] without calling fn

hints: Instead of starting one promise per item, start a few worker loops that each keep taking the next item.

Start a fixed number of worker loops that share one next-index counter, have each store its result at the index it claimed, wait for all the workers, and use a shared failure flag so no new work starts after an error.
Run a fixed number of loops in parallel that each claim the next unclaimed position, store their result at that position, and stop claiming as soon as any call has failed.

drills.title: Bug hunt: mapLimit: async map with bounded concurrency
drills.instructions:
**Bug hunt.** The code in the editor is a plausible first attempt at drill 1, "mapLimit: async map with bounded concurrency". It passes some of the tests, but it has one real bug, the kind a reviewer should catch before it ships.

**Your task.** Find the bug and fix it, changing as little as you can; the tests are the same as drill 1's. The spec is unchanged: Export `mapLimit(items, limit, fn)`. It returns a promise of an array where element i is the result of `await fn(items[i], i)`, and:
- at most `limit` calls of `fn` are in flight at any moment
- results are in INPUT order, whatever order the calls finish in
- if any call rejects, the returned promise rejects with that reason (calls already started may finish, but no NEW call starts after the failure)
- an empty `items` array resolves to `[]`

`limit` is a whole number of 1 or more.

tests.name: results keep input order
never more than limit calls in flight
fn receives the item and its index
tests.code: assert.deepEqual(await mod.mapLimit(['a', 'b'], 1, async (s, i) => s + i), ['a0', 'b1']);

tests.name: a failure rejects and starts no new calls
an empty list resolves to [] without calling fn

drills.explanation:
When one call rejects, its worker stops and the returned promise rejects, but the other workers keep pulling new items, so calls go on starting after the failure (the test opens the gates by hand and sees item 3 start). A shared `failed` flag, set in a catch and checked in the loop condition, stops new work at once.

Only the test "a failure rejects and starts no new calls" fails on the starter; the other four pass, because none of them has a call that rejects. Checking the flag only once before the loop is not enough: a worker must re-check it before every new item, which is why it sits in the `while` condition.
hints: Make one call fail and count how many calls start after the failure.
The failing worker stops, but the other workers keep taking new items.
Record that a call failed in state the workers share, and have every worker check it before taking the next item.
